Title: How to deal with Peoples failure to Pay for things

Messages.Author: Brian Skelly
Messages.Body:
As i am going to be the Judge of a National Qualifier im going to ask
a couple of Questions that bug me:

If player A plays Anarch Revolt and Player B forgets to pay before the
start of Player C's turn.

1. Do you Punish Player B with warnings for failure to pay?
2. Is it on me to make sure everyone Pays?

Also, in regards to Automatic vs Choice:

If Player A has Basic Group 1 Leandro, and Player B gets all the way
to their Transfer Phase and has not yet paid the pool to be able to
Transfer?

1. Because it is a forced thing, does he get to choose then?
2. Has he forfited his rights to transfer?

And now a generic one,

What about cards that cost you pool during your Untap (i.e. Fame) and
every player forgets or only some forget.

1. Do you make them pay?
2. Do you warn etc?

I am just after some opinions, I know as the Judge I have the final
say but some of our local players have asked so i thought i would ask
here.

Thankyou :)

-- Brian

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
In message <3c8a815e.04060...@posting.google.com>,
br...@luvbite.com (Brian Skelly) mumbled something about:

>As i am going to be the Judge of a National Qualifier im going to ask
>a couple of Questions that bug me:
>
>If player A plays Anarch Revolt and Player B forgets to pay before the
>start of Player C's turn.
>
>1. Do you Punish Player B with warnings for failure to pay?
>2. Is it on me to make sure everyone Pays?

It's on player A, primarily, and everyone else at the table.

I'd take it from player B's pool at the time of rememberage. If it
would oust him due to some whack conflict of interest, then a rewind
might be necessary; but I'd only consider rewinding if it would oust him
and that would significantly change his turn (ie, he bled C for 6 during
that turn and only had 1 pool in his untap; or he had 2 pool in his
untap, Blood Dolled 1 off, and purchased a .44; etc). These should be
rare though.

>Also, in regards to Automatic vs Choice:
>
>If Player A has Basic Group 1 Leandro, and Player B gets all the way
>to their Transfer Phase and has not yet paid the pool to be able to
>Transfer?
>
>1. Because it is a forced thing, does he get to choose then?
>2. Has he forfited his rights to transfer?

He must make the choice; failure to remember that there's a choice to be
made doesn't make the choice for him. He gets to choose whether or not
to pay.

If he does it twice, I'd warn him. :)

>And now a generic one,
>
>What about cards that cost you pool during your Untap (i.e. Fame) and
>every player forgets or only some forget.
>
>1. Do you make them pay?

Make them pay and optionally warn them as well for repeat infractions.

-- Derek

Messages.Author: Izaak
Messages.Body:
> If player A plays Anarch Revolt and Player B forgets to pay before the
> start of Player C's turn.
>
> 1. Do you Punish Player B with warnings for failure to pay?
> 2. Is it on me to make sure everyone Pays?

1. If he forgets once, he can just pay as soon as you notice. If it
happens all the time, issue a warning.
2. You should keep an eye on that, yes. Usually tables are friendly
enough that players remind each other if they forget.

> Also, in regards to Automatic vs Choice:
>
> If Player A has Basic Group 1 Leandro, and Player B gets all the way
> to their Transfer Phase and has not yet paid the pool to be able to
> Transfer?
>
> 1. Because it is a forced thing, does he get to choose then?

No. Payment must be made during untap.

> 2. Has he forfited his rights to transfer?

Yes.

> And now a generic one,
>
> What about cards that cost you pool during your Untap (i.e. Fame) and
> every player forgets or only some forget.
>
> 1. Do you make them pay?

Just like AR. If they forget (and nobody reminds them) and you notice it
shortly after, make them pay later.

> 2. Do you warn etc?

If one player is forgetting it all the time and constantly has to pay
later, then yes issue a warning. On the other hand, don't warn to soon.
It's still a game and often enough people remind one another of such
events during, or right after the phase it should happen in. Official
warnings can really upset people; just an example that bothered me
personally was this:

I accidentaly replaced a Bum's Rush. I noticed even before I saw the
next card (I had my hand on it and drew it like 1 cm before putting it
back). The judge's response: don't do that again.
The next turn, I played a sideslip at CEL on a 0-damage strike (there
was a Disarm hidden somewhere between the 5 cards on that minion) and
replaced it, causing the official warning yelling (from the OBSERVERS!)
at me and the judge gave me that warning (kinda lead to it by the
observers), which really took the fun out of that game for me.

controller of the Fame and the player who is untapping.

Messages.Author: Aaron
Messages.Body:
OK. Hand size tends to be something that can oscillate alot - what
happens if I forget to replace my WWeF during untap and remember later
during my minion phase. Do I draw it when I remember and if so and its
a Master card and I played no master, can I then retroactively play
it?

Conversely, if I find that I have one card over my hand size what
action should be taken? Does the player discard back to library, to
ash heap, is it random or based on the trust that 'that' card was the
one they picked up last?

What about forced blood *gain* effects (beneficial rather than
detrimental) such as The Rack on a vampire that I forget to move blood
to before I play that Master? Does the 2 blood go on at the point of
rememberance?

Messages.Author: Izaak
Messages.Body:
"Gregory Stuart Pettigrew" <ethe...@sidehack.sat.gweep.net> schreef in
bericht news:2004060112...@sidehack.sat.gweep.net...

> > > 2. Has he forfited his rights to transfer?
> >
> > Yes.
> >
>
> No. As stated before, failure to make a mandatory decision does not
force
> you into either avenue of the decision.

This does not really make sense to me.

Take for example, the Egde.

You are allowed *not* to take pool from the Edge. So, if you forget to
decide whether or not you want to take pool (I can imagine Parity Shift
situations, for example), you, by default, do not take pool. It is not
allowed to gain pool from the edge afterwards, because you forgot.

Leandro is, IMO, not much different. You have to make the decision in
your untap phase. The point of this is of course to force the decision
to be taken ahead instead of seeing what your turn turns out to look
like. For example, I "forget" to pay the pool to get transfers. I play
govern at superior on my 7 cap with 4 pool on it. It gets blocked;
something I had not taken into account. In my influence phase I still
want to make the transfers, but "forgot" to burn a pool to be able to do
so. According to you I can now still burn a pool anyway and can make my
transfers.

This is of course preventable by just forcing every Methusalah to
specifically announce whether or not he's paying for Leandro, but that's
simply not practical, especially once you get past the "influencing out
guys" phase.

In the same line, in my last tournament my prey was controlling Leandro
at the finals table. The judge specifically stated "if you forget to
pay, you're fucked". This would be, according to LSJ's ruling, illegal,
since if I forget, I can still burn the pool afterwards.

Can't his ability just trigger in the influence phase instead? As it is,
it's a pointless exception.

I forget to burn a pool for Bleeding the Vine (and leave it untapped
accidentaly; nobody notices). My prey plays a master. I tap the Vine and
then someone notices I didn't pay. I surely can't pay for it at that
point, can I? What if I was a t 1 pool during my untap phase and gained
some pool during my turn?

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>Take for example, the Egde.
>

>allowed to gain pool from the edge afterwards, because you forgot.
>

>your untap phase.

"You have to ..." The decision is mandatory.

What I don't get is why it's so hard for people to remember Leandro's ability
given what an obvious presence he has. It's the job of everyone at the table
to keep track of these things; someone should be able to notice.

Similarly, in a notice what's going on in the game way, I almost always notice
when someone else keeps the edge (if only that translated to remembering when I
have it). But, since there's supposed to be (in theory, in casual play, I play
with people who allow taking for the edge way late) a penalty for not
remembering, I don't tend to prompt people unless I want them to have more
pool.

>The point of this is of course to force the decision
>to be taken ahead instead of seeing what your turn turns out to look
>like. For example, I "forget" to pay the pool to get transfers. I play
>govern at superior on my 7 cap with 4 pool on it. It gets blocked;
>something I had not taken into account. In my influence phase I still
>want to make the transfers, but "forgot" to burn a pool to be able to do
>so. According to you I can now still burn a pool anyway and can make my
>transfers.

Is that designer intent?

>This is of course preventable by just forcing every Methusalah to
>specifically announce whether or not he's paying for Leandro, but that's
>simply not practical, especially once you get past the "influencing out
>guys" phase.
>
>In the same line, in my last tournament my prey was controlling Leandro
>at the finals table. The judge specifically stated "if you forget to
>pay, you're fucked". This would be, according to LSJ's ruling, illegal,
>since if I forget, I can still burn the pool afterwards.
>
>Can't his ability just trigger in the influence phase instead? As it is,
>it's a pointless exception.
>
>I forget to burn a pool for Bleeding the Vine (and leave it untapped
>accidentaly; nobody notices). My prey plays a master. I tap the Vine and
>then someone notices I didn't pay. I surely can't pay for it at that
>point, can I? What if I was a t 1 pool during my untap phase and gained
>some pool during my turn?

The table should be paying attention. If no one notices something, than the
judge tries to come up with the suitable remedy. When in doubt, see what the
judge thinks and try not to repeat mistakes. For one thing, if the same
mistakes keep getting made, the players should be penalized.

Of course, one of the reasons people repeat mistakes is when they are allowed
takebacks. This is why I understand the infamous LA reputation of adhering
closely to rules.

Messages.Author: Gregory Stuart Pettigrew
Messages.Body:
> Take for example, the Egde.
>

Getting pool from the Edge is optional. Playing a Master Card is optional.
Acting is optional. Forgetting any of those things does not mean you get
to do those things. There are too many optional things for anyone to allow
you to go back and take advantage of them.

Leandro, unlike the Edge, is not A or nothing. It's A or B. Both of which
are rather serious.

> Leandro is, IMO, not much different. You have to make the decision in
> your untap phase. The point of this is of course to force the decision
> to be taken ahead instead of seeing what your turn turns out to look
> like. For example, I "forget" to pay the pool to get transfers. I play
> govern at superior on my 7 cap with 4 pool on it. It gets blocked;
> something I had not taken into account. In my influence phase I still
> want to make the transfers, but "forgot" to burn a pool to be able to do
> so. According to you I can now still burn a pool anyway and can make my
> transfers.
>

Yes, and a good player will recognize the fact that he would not have
"paid the Leandro tax" and act accordingly. Likewise, a good player who
desperately needs another minion and topdecks a Govern will recognize the
fact that he would have "paid the Leandro tax" and burn the pool even if
he doesn't end up using the transfers.

> This is of course preventable by just forcing every Methusalah to
> specifically announce whether or not he's paying for Leandro, but that's
> simply not practical, especially once you get past the "influencing out
> guys" phase.
>

If I have Leandro in play, I ask. That's simply your share of "the Leandro
tax," the least of the burdens he incurs.

> I forget to burn a pool for Bleeding the Vine (and leave it untapped
> accidentaly; nobody notices). My prey plays a master. I tap the Vine and
> then someone notices I didn't pay. I surely can't pay for it at that
> point, can I?

No, you can't pay for it at that point. But you can't tap it at that
point. Bleeding the Vine, like Leandro, is A or B, not A or nothing. You
have to go back and retroactively have spent or tapped.

>What if I was a t 1 pool during my untap phase and gained
> some pool during my turn?
>

Then a good player will be honest and tap it retroactively.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Aaron wrote:
> OK. Hand size tends to be something that can oscillate alot - what
> happens if I forget to replace my WWeF during untap and remember later
> during my minion phase. Do I draw it when I remember and if so and its
> a Master card and I played no master, can I then retroactively play
> it?

You can't play it outside of your master phase.
You could, judge allowing, rewind to your untap phase to draw the card,
and then, master in hand, play the master card during your master phase.
Assuming not "too much" has transpired in the interim.

> Conversely, if I find that I have one card over my hand size what
> action should be taken? Does the player discard back to library, to
> ash heap, is it random or based on the trust that 'that' card was the
> one they picked up last?

Judge's discretion. If the player asserts that she knows which card
was overdrawn and the judge believes her to be in earnest, then that
card is returned. It should be shuffled into the library, assuming
no one has had cause to discover that it was on top of the library
via some card effect.

> What about forced blood *gain* effects (beneficial rather than
> detrimental) such as The Rack on a vampire that I forget to move blood
> to before I play that Master? Does the 2 blood go on at the point of
> rememberance?

Beneficial, detrimental - it's all handled the same way - rewind if
able/convenient. Restore/maintain balance if not.

Messages.Author: Chris Shorb
Messages.Body:
Hey Mike -

Regarding Leandro, in Los Angeles (IIRC), if you don't declare a choice and move
to your master phase, it is assumed that your choice was "Not Pay". Have you guys
changed that behavior up in Glendale? By being punished in game, you will be sure
to remember next time. I don't see why it's that hard to play that way, and it's
way better and more clear.

In other words, if you don't declare, then you are in effect declaring "no" to any
given mandatory decision. If you forget, well, don't forget next time. There
should never be a benefit for forgetting, and as far as I can tell, letting
someone "rewind" and pay the 1 pool tax to get an influence phase is a reward for
forgetting.

Otherwise, I agree with Derek.

best -

While it is OK to do this in a friendly game as 'reminder punishment', it is
innapropriate for a tournament (see Derek's and LSJ's posts). Still, just
once more:

The choices are A and B, not Yes and No. In this case you could put the
choices as 'Not to forfeit the influence phase' and 'Not to pay 1 pool'. So,
which 'No' is it then?

> If you forget, well, don't forget next time. There
> should never be a benefit for forgetting, and as far as I can tell, letting
> someone "rewind" and pay the 1 pool tax to get an influence phase is a reward for

If the delay in the choice gives a significant advantage, the judge is
allowed to make any adjustments necessary to compensate.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Chris Shorb wrote:
> Regarding Leandro, in Los Angeles (IIRC), if you don't declare a choice and move
> to your master phase, it is assumed that your choice was "Not Pay". Have you guys
> changed that behavior up in Glendale? By being punished in game, you will be sure

They probably have, if it was done otherwise, in order to merge with the
official rulings. There is no assumed choice for Leandro, contesting, etc.
The player is required to choose, but there is no default (since the choice
is required - no default is needed).

> to remember next time. I don't see why it's that hard to play that way, and it's
> way better and more clear.

Not more clear - neither choice is given as a default.
Not way better, since it muddles the paradigm and can lead to confusion in
other no-default choice cases.

> In other words, if you don't declare, then you are in effect declaring "no" to any
> given mandatory decision. If you forget, well, don't forget next time. There

"No (I won't choose)" isn't the same as "I choose A" or "I choose B".

> should never be a benefit for forgetting, and as far as I can tell, letting
> someone "rewind" and pay the 1 pool tax to get an influence phase is a reward for
> forgetting.

No. It is a pool loss. If it can be shown that the player is gaining some
sort of advantage (over having made the decision herself at the time), then
the judge should rectify that with the appropriate penalty. That penalty
could be the loss of a pool (effecting one choice), the loss of transfers
(effecting another choice), or something else, as appropriate. In practice,
it would be hard to argue for an advantage in Leandro's case.

Messages.Author: Mike Courtois
Messages.Body:
Chris Shorb <chr...@vtesinla.org> wrote in message news:<410F2736...@vtesinla.org>...

> Hey Mike -
>
> Regarding Leandro, in Los Angeles (IIRC), if you don't declare a choice and move
> to your master phase, it is assumed that your choice was "Not Pay". Have you guys
> changed that behavior up in Glendale?

This came up quite awhile ago in an LA tourny. I ALWAYS argued with
the Judge at the time that the player must be aloud to decide at the
time the mistake is discovered. The Judge (Paul) did not agree and
forced him to skip his turn. That's the Judges right, and that's how
he judged that call. I'm ok with that.

Different Judges will see/make decisions differently. In an effort
to make things as uniform as possible **I** try to judge as close to
LSJ's style as possible. Simply because it is as close to a uniform
standard as we will ever come too. Others are free to judge as they
like on these affairs and I believe the Judge has the right to judge
as he/she sees fit as long as the Tourny rules are follwed.
If you watch sports the ref's will make some calls and let some go,
the next night can have different refs which will make compleatly
different calls. It's no different in VtES. We do talk often on
judging calls to see if we can be consistant but there are time when
our philosophies will differ. I think I remember LSJ telling me once,
"Judge the way you think you should Judge." I took that to mean at the
end of the day if you'er the Judge It's ok to make the call whatever
it is, just be able to back it up. It's also ok to make a wrong call,
just find the correct answer latter so you won't make the same mistake
again.

Back to the inital question, **I** would let him decide at the time
the mistake is found and if it continued I would warn him, and if it
continued I would not give him the option of paying.

***JediMike***

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
One of the issues that came up at Powerbase: LA last weekend was
another interesting point. Someone had put out a copy of Millicent
Smith, Puritan Vampire Hunter. The card was going around the table
normally. Then, on the second or third go-'round, my prey moved
her to my table space without bothering to notify me. And he
didn't really do a good job of placing the card, either. It was
up in the corner, sort of halfway between his space and mine where
I had no reason to look. It was late, I was tired from the long
drive the night before and not getting much sleep, and in general
I can be a very spacy person. ("Gee, Fred. I see that once again
you have opted NOT to take your optional pool from the edge."...
"DOH!")

Anyway, to make a long story short, unaware that Millicent was
visiting my realms, I acted away, got intercepted not once but
twice. My prey and I had combat both times. I ended my turn and
during my predator's turn, we discovered the error. No one at the
table had noticed Millicent the whole time. At that point, we
called the judge over. Her ruling was that the first vampire that
got intercepted had to be burned, and that it was my responsibility
as much as anyone else's to notice where Millicent was. Of course,
at that point, it was absolutely impossible to recontruct what
would have happened had my first vampire been burned, so after
mulling it over a bit, I just consented to burn it and go on with
the game and everyone else at the table seemed OK with that.

As such an event had multiple causes, I will concede, the judge
had a point. None the less, what bothers me about the scenario
is that it gives my prey an incentive to be very coy and quiet
about the act of moving Millicent. In this particular situation,
I don't think the guy did it on purpose. But I already have a
huge pet peeve about people who take actions and play cards and
so forth that need to get everyone's attention and they don't bother
to be very assertive about such things. ("Hello, is it my turn
yet?" "Oh, yes, my turn was over 5 minutes ago - I was wondering
why you were waiting." "Well, because you never SAID anything!")
It becomes egregious when they play things that clearly affect
me (e.g. my prey playing a Rack on his blood doll). Millicent
Smith is the mother of all effects that affect your turn, so it
seems to me that your prey should shout at you about it as it
moves - not be allowed to slip it into your space when you're not
looking.

The judge said something that I find even more disturbing: that had
my prey forgotten to move Millicent at all, her ruling would be the
same, based on the same criteria. That would be a situation that
places the principal of not letting people escape their situation just
because they forgot something (in such a case, I would have forgotten
that my prey's Millicent should move, as would he) squarely against
another principal that I thought was important: that one should never
gain a distinct advantage from one's failure to play the game
correctly (my prey would be allowed to wipe out one of his predator's
vampires through his own forgetfulness). In such situations, I was
always of the opinion that the latter consideration is the important
point. I'd like to hear an opinion on all this.

Fred

I personally wouldn't want to see any players stealthily moving or not
moving Millicent at all as a ploy to get their predator's vampires
burned. If I wasn't convinced as a judge that Millicent wasn't openly
and clearly moved I wouldn't burn your vamp. My version of what is
sufficiently open and clear is going to be different from another
judge's version, of course.

-Robert

Ah, OK, that was a pretty distinct misunderstanding, then, yes.
The whole point I was trying to make to you was about, "At what point
do you consider the behavior of the prey in terms of not calling
attention to the movement of Millicent (or very meager attempts to)
which works to his own benefit?" I sure thought your answer was, "At
_no_ point - you (meaning me, in this situation) also have a duty to
know where Millicent is supposed to be at any given moment." And to
back up your point, I could have sworn you'd stated that my prey could
have completely forgotten to move Millicent at all and your ruling
would have been the same. That made sense to me in that it would be
the most extreme example of poor behavior on the part of the prey
and thus represents a coherent position on the matter. I just found
it to be a very disturbing position. Now I'm not sure what you meant.

In any event, as I said at the time, it wasn't so much about that game.
I has having a pretty rough game before I got ousted so what's losing
another vampire? To me, this issue kind of dovetails with some other
things I've noticed about the LA tournament scene having to do with
(roughly) with the issue of not taking back actions once played. It's
the sort of thing I would expect from any of the LA judges. Perhaps
I'll post about it under a different thread sometime because I think
it's an interesting issue. (Then and again, if I think it's interesting,
no doubt it will bore most normal people half to death.)

Fred

> So your extending the meaning of 'effect' to include the turn phase's?

No. Simply applying 1.6.1.6.
The acting player must "pass" when it comes time for her to play the
next effect or pass in order for the phase to end (and that "pass"
must be followed by "passes" from all the other players as well, in
the order indicated by 1.6.1.6.) When that happens, the phase ends. If
that phase that ended was the discard phase, the last phase in the
turn, then the turn ends.


